The final pixel color $S^{(SG)}$ is computed by integrating the product of the BRDF, incident radiance, and cosine term [S3, unofficial]:

The claim states that the final pixel color $S^{(SG)}$ is computed by integrating the product of the BRDF, incident radiance, and cosine term. Source [S3], specifically in the 'Spherical Gaussian Shading' section and Equation (6), explicitly defines the final pixel color $S^{(SG)}$ as the integral over the sphere $S^2$ of the product of the SG BRDF ($f_r^{(SG)}$), the incident radiance ($L_i^{(SG)}$), and the approximated cosine foreshortening term ($G_c$). The text confirms: 'Regrouping all terms, the final pixel color can be computed as: ... integral of f_r^{(SG)} ... L_i^{(SG)} ... G_c ... dω_i'. Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.

MC is better for mirror-like objects (low roughness) where high frequencies are preserved, but SG is more efficient for moderate-to-high roughness [S3, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that Monte Carlo (MC) 'targets more mirror-like objects and can better approximate higher frequencies in the integrand' (Section 3.4). It also notes that Spherical Gaussians (SG) are 'more robust to roughness variations' and that visual comparisons reveal SGs can 'correctly approximate direct illumination at moderate-to-high roughness' (Figure 2 caption and Section 4). Furthermore, the text explains that MC is 'more expensive to compute' while SG is used to 'accelerate rendering' (Section 4), supporting the claim that SG is more efficient. The claim accurately reflects these distinctions found in the source text.
